sentences.text: This crocodylomorph is recognized by its laterally bulged snout edges, a feature most prominent near an enlarged maxillary tooth.
One species possessed a highly enlarged, forward-pointing first dentary tooth called an incisiform, resembling rodent incisors.
The largest known skull measures 130 millimeters in length.
While one species reached 81 cm in length, another could grow up to one meter.
The genus was named in 1959 based on fossils from the Santana Group in Brazil.
It was first described in that same year as A. gomesii from the Santana Formation.
The holotype specimen 423-R, consisting of a single skull articulated with part of a lower jaw, is housed in Rio de Janeiro.
A species named A. wegeneri was described in 1981 from Early Cretaceous deposits in Niger, Africa.
Another species, A. tsangatsangana, was described in 2006 from Late Cretaceous deposits on the island of Madagascar.
A fifth species, A. patagonicus, was described in 2000 from a specimen found in Patagonia, Argentina.
There are currently seven recognized species within the genus Araripesuchus.
Araripesuchus likely spent more time on land than in water, suggested by its non-keeled osteoderms, long limb bones, and upright posture.
Research indicates the animal grew slowly with annual growth interruptions, evidenced by lines of arrested growth in its bones.
Araripesuchus is generally classified as a notosuchian within the clade Mesoeucrocodylia.
Recent phylogenetic analyses generally place Araripesuchus as a basal notosuchian.
Some phylogenetic analyses suggest Araripesuchus is more closely related to the Neosuchia clade, which includes modern crocodilians.
However, many recent analyses place Araripesuchus as a basal notosuchian.
The taxonomic classification of Araripesuchus within the suborder Notosuchia is sometimes marked as uncertain.
The genus was originally assigned to the family Uruguaysuchidae by Price in 1959.
In 2000, Ortega et al. and other studies placed Araripesuchus outside of Notosuchia following the description of A. patagonicus.
A 2011 phylogenetic analysis by Soto et al. united Araripesuchus with Uruguaysuchus, re-establishing the family Uruguaysuchidae.
Araripesuchus lived during the Cretaceous period, approximately 125 to 66 million years ago.
The animal lived from the Aptian to the Maastrichtian, between 121.4 and 66 million years ago.
Fossils found in South America and Africa suggest a Gondwanan origin for Araripesuchus.
Some recent analyses question the validity of the genus Araripesuchus by placing A. wegeneri as a sister taxon to Anatosuchus.
